Why cash under the mattress loses value

When prices of goods rise over time, economists call it **inflation**. If a paint of garri cost less last year than it does today, that is inflation at work. The important lesson is this: ₦10,000 kept in a tin at home is still ₦10,000 next year, but it buys less. Cash at home can also be stolen, burnt or eaten by rats, and it is easy to spend on impulse. That is why later in this course we compare safer places to keep savings.
Worked example: the same money, two choices
For example, Ngozi sells pepper soup and keeps her savings in a tin at home. Her neighbour Halima saves the same amount in a bank savings account.
Both save about ₦5,000 every week for a year, which is about ₦260,000 (52 weeks x ₦5,000).
Twice during the year Ngozi takes from the tin for things that were not planned, such as a party outfit, and she does not put the money back. She ends the year with about ₦190,000.
Halima's money is not in front of her. It needs a transfer to spend, which gives her time to think. She ends with her full ₦260,000 plus a small amount of interest.
Both women face rising prices, so neither amount buys as much as it would have a year earlier.
The biggest difference was not interest. It was that Halima's money was harder to spend on impulse and safe from theft. Where you keep savings changes how much you keep.

Needs vs wants: deciding what comes first

A **need** is something you must have to live safely, stay healthy and keep earning: basic food, safe shelter, clean water, essential healthcare, basic clothing, school fees for your children, and the transport or tools you need for work. A **want** is something that makes life nicer but you could live without, or delay, for now: a new phone when your old one works, aso ebi for every event, eating out, the latest shoes.

The line is not always simple, because many items have a need part and a want part. Food is a need, but rice and stew at home costs far less than buying food outside every day. Transport to work is a need, but a ride-hailing car when a bus would do is partly a want. Your phone may be a need for your business, but an expensive new model is a want.
A person choosing between two options
Before you buy, pause and ask: is this a need, or a want I can delay?
The three-question test
Ask: what happens if I do not buy this today? If the answer is that my family goes hungry, falls sick, loses shelter or I cannot work, it is a need.
Ask: is there a cheaper version that meets the same need? The basic version is the need. The extra cost is the want.
Ask: can this wait 30 days? If it can wait, it is probably a want. Write it on a "wants list" instead of buying it now.

Wants are not bad

This lesson is not about never enjoying anything. Wants give life joy, and cutting every one usually fails after a few weeks. The goal is to **pay for needs first, save next, and then enjoy wants with what is left**, knowingly. A small planned treat is better than a big unplanned one that leaves you short for rent.
The 30-day wants list

Impulse buying happens when we see something and buy it on the spot, often because of a sales pitch, a WhatsApp status or a friend's purchase. A simple defence is the **30-day wants list**. When you feel like buying a non-essential item, write it down with the price and the date. If you still want it after 30 days and you have the money without touching savings or needs, buy it. You will find that many items drop off the list on their own.
Handling social and family pressure

Weddings, burials, naming ceremonies and family requests are real parts of life. Decide in advance how much you can give each month for events and family support, and keep to it. It is fine to say: "I cannot buy the aso ebi this time, but I will come and celebrate with you." Giving within your plan protects your own children's needs.
Needs change with your situation

Shopping habits matter too. Go to the market with a written list and a set amount of cash or a set transfer limit. Buying staples such as rice, beans and oil in larger quantities, when you can afford to and can store them safely, often costs less per cup than buying small amounts daily. Some women share a bulk bag with a trusted neighbour and split the cost. Avoid shopping when you are hungry or rushed, because that is when wants slip into the basket.

A need for one family may be a want for another. A generator may be a need for a woman who runs a frozen food business, but a want for someone whose work does not depend on power. Be honest with yourself about your own situation, not what neighbours do. Review your needs list every few months, because children grow, rent changes and businesses change.

Gross income and take-home income

If you earn a salary, your **gross income** is the full amount on your offer letter. Your **take-home** or net income is what reaches your account after deductions such as tax (PAYE), pension contribution and any loan repayments taken by your employer. Always plan with take-home income, because that is the money you can actually use.

For a business, the money you collect from customers is not all income for your family. Part of it must go back to buy stock and pay costs. Your real income is your **profit**: sales minus business costs. A common mistake is to spend sales money at home and then find there is nothing left to restock. Keep business money and household money separate, even if it is only two envelopes or two bank accounts.

Planning with irregular income

When income changes month to month, plan with a **careful average**, not your best month. Look back at the last three to six months, write down what came in each month, and use the lowest month or the average of the lower months as your planning figure. In good months, the extra goes first to savings or to a buffer that tops up lean months.
Worked example: finding a safe monthly figure
For example, Funke runs a small food canteen in Ibadan. Her profit (after buying ingredients and paying her helper) over six months was approximately as follows.
Total for six months: about ₦560,000. Average: about ₦93,000 per month (₦560,000 divided by 6).
Her lowest month was about ₦70,000.
She chooses ₦80,000 as her safe planning figure, between the lowest month and the average.
In any month she makes more than ₦80,000, she moves the extra into a separate savings account as a buffer.
Funke now budgets her home spending on about ₦80,000. In a weak month the buffer fills the gap, so rent and school fees are never in danger.

If you run a business, choose a fixed amount to transfer to your personal account on the same day each week or month. This turns irregular sales into a steadier household income and protects your stock money.

Before spending any of it, decide how much will cover the months ahead, how much goes to savings, and how much is truly free. A farmer who receives most of her year's income at harvest should divide it into monthly amounts so the family is not short in the planting season.

Use one page per month in a notebook, or a note on your phone. Write the date, the source and the amount every time money comes in. Bank and mobile money apps such as Opay, Moniepoint, PalmPay or your bank app show a transaction history, which helps, but cash income must be written down by hand or it disappears from your picture. Irregular expenses cause the most stress, because they feel like emergencies even though we knew they were coming. Annual rent is the classic example. The fix is to divide each yearly cost by 12 and set that amount aside every month. We will do this in the worked example below.

Choose your tool: a small notebook you carry, the notes app on your phone, or a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets.
Every time you spend, write the date, what you bought and the amount. Do it immediately, or at the end of each day at the latest.
Include cash, transfers, POS payments, airtime and data, and money given to others.
At the end of each week, group the spending into categories such as food, transport, utilities, children, business, giving and personal.
At the end of the month, add each category and compare it with what you expected.

Small leaks, big holes

A leak is a small, frequent cost that feels harmless. Common leaks include buying drinks and snacks daily, paying extra for small data bundles instead of a monthly plan, bank charges from many tiny transfers, and buying foodstuff in very small quantities at a higher unit price. One leak on its own seems minor. Multiplied by 30 days, it can be the cost of a term's school uniform.
Worked example: leaks and yearly costs
For example, Blessing, a teacher in Port Harcourt, tracked her spending for one month. Amounts are approximate.
She found she spent about ₦800 a day on drinks and snacks at work. Over 22 working days that is about ₦17,600 a month.
She bought small daily data bundles costing about ₦8,000 in the month. A monthly plan with similar data would have cost noticeably less.
Her annual rent is about ₦480,000. Divided by 12, that is about ₦40,000 she should set aside every month.
Her children's school fees are about ₦90,000 per term, three terms a year: ₦270,000 a year, or about ₦22,500 a month.

By packing a drink from home on most days and switching to a monthly data plan, Blessing freed about ₦15,000 a month. Setting aside about ₦62,500 monthly for rent and fees means those payments no longer feel like emergencies.
Watch for unexplained debits

When you check your bank or mobile money history, look for charges you do not recognise, subscriptions you forgot, or transfers you did not make. Report any you did not authorise to your bank immediately through its official app, branch or customer care line, never through a number someone sends you.
What your tracking tells you

If writing every item feels too hard, try the **envelope count** instead. Start the week with a set amount of cash in an envelope for daily spending, and note how much is left each evening. For digital spending, open your bank or mobile money app every Sunday and read through the week's debits. Both methods show you the same truth: where the money actually went, compared with where you thought it went. Choose the method you will actually keep doing.

Saving means keeping part of today's money for tomorrow. It sounds simple, but when money is tight it can feel impossible. The secret is to give your savings a clear **job**. Money with a job is much easier to protect than money that is just "extra".
Savings do three main jobs:
**Protect** the family from shocks: illness, a job loss, a broken shop freezer, a sudden death in the family. This is your emergency fund, covered in Lesson 4.
**Reach goals** that cost more than one month's income: rent, school fees, a sewing machine, a deep freezer for a business, a plot of land.
**Seize opportunities**: buying stock in bulk at a good price, paying for a training course, starting a side business without borrowing.

A good savings goal is **specific**. "I want to save money" is a wish. "I will save ₦150,000 for a new industrial sewing machine by 31 March" is a goal. It has an amount, a purpose and a date, so you can work out the weekly or monthly saving needed.

Pay yourself first

Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month. Usually, nothing is left. **Pay yourself first** turns this around: the moment money comes in, move your savings amount out before you spend on anything else. Treat savings like a bill you must pay. Even a small fixed amount, saved first and every time, beats a large amount you only hope to save.

Many banks and mobile money apps let you set an **automatic transfer** or a locked target savings plan on a fixed date. If your salary arrives on the 25th, set the transfer for the 25th. You never see the money in your spending account, so you do not miss it.
Worked example: working backwards from a goal
For example, Kemi sells provisions in Abeokuta and wants a deep freezer to add frozen chicken and fish to her shop. The freezer costs about ₦300,000 (approximate, prices change).
She sets a date 10 months away.
₦300,000 divided by 10 months is about ₦30,000 a month.
That is about ₦7,000 a week (₦30,000 divided by about 4.3 weeks).
She already saves ₦3,000 a week, so she needs about ₦4,000 more each week.
From her tracking, she cuts daily take-away lunch (about ₦2,500 a week) and buys her shop stock in larger, cheaper quantities (about ₦1,500 a week saved).
Kemi now saves about ₦7,000 a week into a locked target savings plan. She also checks the freezer price again before buying, because prices may rise during the 10 months.
Plan for rising prices
If your goal is many months away, the price may go up before you buy. Add a margin (for example 10 to 20 percent) to the target, or check the price every few months and adjust your weekly saving.
Small amounts really add up

Do not wait until you can save a big amount. Saving ₦500 a day is about ₦15,000 a month and about ₦180,000 in a year. Starting small builds the habit, and the habit is what matters most. When income rises, increase the amount. A good rule is to save part of every increase: if your pay or profit goes up by ₦10,000, save at least half of that rise before lifestyle swallows it.

If you are paid daily, as many traders and artisans are, save daily too. Put a fixed amount aside at the end of each working day before counting what is left for home. A small locked box kept away from the shop, emptied into the bank every week, works well for cash businesses.

Saving also changes how you feel. Women who have even a small amount set aside often describe more peace of mind and more confidence when talking with family about money. Savings give you choices: you can say no to a bad loan, or say yes to a good opportunity.

The **Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)** protects depositors if a licensed bank fails. If your bank collapses, NDIC pays insured depositors back up to a set maximum per depositor per bank. The limit is different for commercial banks and for microfinance banks, and it has been changed over the years, so check the current figure on the NDIC website before relying on it. Money in an unlicensed scheme has **no** NDIC protection.

Find the full registered name of the bank or company, not just the app name.
Check the CBN website for its list of licensed banks and other financial institutions.
For apps, read the "About" page: genuine ones name their licence or the licensed bank that holds your money.
If a platform promises investment returns, check that it is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria.
Search the company name with words like "scam" or "complaint" and read what real customers report.

Each pot has a place that suits its job: quick access for emergencies, a lock for rent, and a longer-term option for school fees.
Red flags for savings offers

Be very careful with anyone promising unusually high, guaranteed returns, paying you to bring in new members, asking you to pay into a personal account, or pressuring you to act fast. These are classic signs of a ponzi scheme, which we cover in Module 4. Licensed banks do not ask for your PIN, password or OTP.
Keep savings separate from spending

Whatever option you choose, keep savings in a **different account** from the one you spend from. Many people open a second account at the same bank and do not request a debit card for it. This small barrier gives you time to think before withdrawing. If you use a mobile money wallet for daily spending, keep only spending money there and move savings out.

Remember that interest is only part of the story. A higher rate means nothing if the provider is not genuine, or if the rules make it impossible to get your money in a real emergency. **Safety first, access second, returns third** is a sensible order for most beginners.

Long before banks reached every town, Nigerian women saved together. The Yoruba call it **ajo** or **esusu**, in the north it is often **adashe**, and the Igbo have **isusu**. These groups work because members trust each other and the regular contribution creates discipline. They remain popular because they are simple, local and require no paperwork. But they also carry real risks, so it is worth understanding them well.
How a rotating group works

In a **rotating savings group**, a fixed number of members each contribute the same amount at each meeting. At every round, one member collects the whole pot. The rotation continues until everyone has collected once. Nobody earns interest, but each member receives a large lump sum at some point, which is hard to get by saving alone.

Worked example: a monthly ajo
For example, ten market women in Ibadan agree to contribute about ₦20,000 each month for ten months.

Bisi must keep paying ₦20,000 every month until month 10, even though she has already collected.
Over ten months, every member pays in ₦200,000 and receives ₦200,000.
Early collectors get an interest-free advance; late collectors are effectively saving. The system only works if everyone keeps paying after collecting.
The daily collector

Another common type is the **daily or weekly collector**, often called an alajo or esusu collector. Traders pay a small amount each day, and the collector returns the total at the end of the month. In many arrangements the collector keeps one day's contribution each month as a fee. For example, if you contribute ₦1,000 a day for 31 days, you might receive ₦30,000 back. Ask about the fee clearly before you start.
The real risks
**The collector disappears** with members' money. There is usually no insurance and recovering the money is difficult.
**A member stops paying after collecting.** Later members then receive less or nothing.
**Loss to theft or fire** when cash is kept at home.
**Poor records**, leading to disputes about who paid what.
**No interest**, so inflation reduces the value of money saved for many months.
Protect yourself in any saving group
Join only groups of people you know well and can find. Never join a group that promises more than members put in, or one where you must recruit others to get paid; that is a ponzi scheme, not ajo.
Rules that make a group safer
Write the rules down: amount, dates, order of collection, penalty for late payment, and what happens if someone leaves.
Keep a record book signed at every meeting, or a shared spreadsheet, showing every payment.
Choose a treasurer and a second person to check the records together.
Where possible, keep group money in a group bank account that needs two signatories, not in one person's house.
Put long-standing, trusted members early in the rotation only if the group agrees, and ask early collectors for a guarantor.
Cooperative societies: the more formal step

A **cooperative society** is a member-owned group, such as a staff cooperative or a market traders' cooperative, that can be registered with the cooperative department of your state government. Registered cooperatives have bylaws, elected officers, accounts that can be audited, and often offer members savings plus loans at agreed rates. Registration does not remove all risk, so attend meetings, read the annual accounts and ask questions.

An **emergency fund** is money kept aside only for real, unexpected problems. It is the first and most important savings pot, because without it every surprise becomes a crisis, and crises push families into expensive loans, selling assets cheaply, or pulling children out of school.

How much do you need?

A common guideline from personal finance educators is to aim for **three to six months of essential expenses**. Essential expenses are the needs from your tracking: food, rent share, transport to work, utilities, school costs and medicine. If your income is irregular, or you are the only earner, lean towards the higher end.

That full amount can feel very large, so break it into stages. First save a **starter fund**, for example one month of essentials or a fixed amount you can reach in a few months. Then keep building towards three months, and later six.
Worked example: setting the target
For example, Amaka is a single mother in Enugu. From her tracking, her essential monthly expenses are approximately as follows.

Total essentials: about ₦130,000 per month.
Starter target (one month): about ₦130,000.
Full target (three months): about ₦390,000. Long-term (six months): about ₦780,000.

Amaka now has clear milestones. Each one makes her family safer, even before she reaches the full target.
A protective shield
An emergency fund shields your family's plans when something unexpected happens.
Where to keep it

Emergency money must be **safe** and **reachable within a day or two**, but not so easy to reach that you spend it on everyday things. A separate savings account at a licensed bank, without a debit card attached, is a common choice. Avoid locking it in a plan you cannot break, and never put it in investments that can lose value or in an informal scheme.
Make it harder to touch
Give the account a name in your banking app such as "Emergency only". Some women ask a trusted person to be the one who reminds them of the rule before any withdrawal.
Finding the money to start

If you feel there is nothing left to save, look back at your tracking from Module 1. Most families can find a starting amount from three places. First, one or two leaks, such as daily snacks or small data bundles. Second, a one-off amount, such as part of a bonus, a gift or a good sales week, which can give the fund a quick head start. Third, a small side income, such as selling items you no longer use. Even ₦2,000 a week is about ₦104,000 in a year.

Family pressure is a real threat to emergency funds. Relatives may ask for help with costs that are not true emergencies. You can still help within your giving budget, while keeping the emergency fund for your own household's shocks. It can help to keep the balance private.
Using it and rebuilding it
When an emergency happens, pause and confirm it is truly unplanned and necessary.
Take only what you need, and keep the receipt or a note.
Write down how much you took out.
Restart saving the next month, and temporarily put extra towards rebuilding the fund before other goals.

Using the fund is not failure. It is exactly what it is for. The only mistake is not rebuilding it. Many families also discover, after the first emergency, that they need a bigger fund than they thought, which is useful information.

Some emergencies can be reduced before they happen. Basic health insurance, such as a state health insurance scheme or an employer plan, can lower hospital costs. Keeping copies of important documents, keeping your phone protected and servicing equipment you depend on for work all make shocks smaller. Ask what is available in your state and what it really covers before you pay.

Turn your money picture into a plan. You will choose a budgeting method, build a full monthly budget, live on it with simple weekly habits, and adjust it calmly when income falls or prices rise.
What a budget is and three simple ways to make one
Explain a budget as a plan made before the month begins

Choose the budgeting method that fits your income and habits

A **budget** is a plan for your money, made **before** you spend it. It says: this month, this much is coming in, and this is exactly where it will go. Tracking (Module 1) looks back at what happened. A budget looks forward and tells your money what to do. Together they form a loop: plan, spend, track, compare, improve.

A budget is not a punishment or a sign that you are poor. Businesses, governments and wealthy families all use budgets. It simply means you decide in advance, calmly, instead of deciding under pressure at the market or when a relative calls.

Method 1: the 50/30/20 guideline

A popular starting point divides take-home income into three parts: about **50 percent for needs**, **30 percent for wants**, and **20 percent for savings and extra debt repayment**. It is easy to remember and gives a quick check on whether spending is balanced.

It is a guideline, not a law. For many Nigerian households, especially where food and rent take a large share of income, needs may be 60, 70 or even 80 percent. That is not failure. The adjusted version might be 70 percent needs, 10 percent wants and 20 percent savings, or 75, 15 and 10 to start. The key idea is to protect a **fixed share for savings** and to keep wants limited and planned.

Method 2: zero-based budget

In a **zero-based budget**, you give every naira a job until income minus planned spending and saving equals zero. Zero does not mean you spend everything; savings is one of the jobs. This method is very clear and works well for people who like detail and have a fairly steady income.
Method 3: envelopes or pots

The **envelope method** puts money for each category into its own envelope (for cash) or its own pot or sub-account (for digital money). When the food envelope is empty, food spending stops until next month, or you move money from a want envelope. Many bank and mobile money apps now let you create named savings pots, which works the same way.

Budgeting with irregular income

If your income changes from month to month, budget with your safe planning figure from Module 1, not your hope. Some traders budget week by week instead of month by month: each Friday they count the week's profit, move savings first, set aside the weekly share of rent and fees, and then plan the coming week's food and transport. Any money above the plan goes to the buffer that protects lean weeks. The method is the same; only the time period changes.

Another approach for irregular earners is to rank budget lines in order and fund them one by one as money arrives: first savings and food, then rent savings, then transport, then the rest. In a weak month, the lines at the bottom wait. In a strong month, every line is funded and the extra tops up the buffer.
Pick one method and try it for three months

Every method works if you use it. Choose the one that feels most natural, try it for three months, then adjust. Many women combine them: an adapted 50/30/20 to set the shares, and envelopes or pots to stick to them.

Whatever method you choose, write your budget down. A budget kept only in your head is easily forgotten when pressure comes. A page in your notebook or a simple phone spreadsheet is enough. In the next lesson you will build your first full monthly budget, line by line.

When the numbers do not balance

If your planned spending is higher than your income, you have three choices: spend less, earn more, or both. Start with wants. Then look at variable needs for cheaper options: cooking at home more, buying staples in bulk, walking short distances, choosing a cheaper data plan. If it still does not balance, the gap is telling you something important: income may need to rise, through extra hours, a side business or better pricing in your trade. Do not balance a budget by borrowing for everyday needs; that only moves the problem to next month with interest added.

Look closely at the food line in Tolu's budget. It is the biggest variable need, so small changes there make a big difference. Planning a weekly menu, buying staples such as rice, beans, garri and oil in larger quantities when cash allows, and cooking larger pots that last two days can reduce it noticeably without eating less. The same thinking applies to transport: combining errands into one trip saves fares every week.

Notice also that rent appears as a monthly line even though the landlord is paid once a year. This is the most important habit in the whole budget. The money moves every month into a separate rent pot, so when the rent date comes, the full amount is already waiting.
Couples and shared households

If you share money with a spouse or family, build the budget together where possible. Agree who pays which lines and how savings will be held. Clear agreements prevent misunderstandings and help everyone pull in the same direction.
Keep it simple

Your first budget does not need to be perfect. Use round numbers. Ten to twelve categories are enough. The first month will show you where your guesses were wrong, and that is how you improve. A simple paper budget that you look at every week is far more useful than a detailed spreadsheet you never open.

If you prefer a phone, a free spreadsheet app like Google Sheets lets you set up columns for category, planned and actual, with a formula to subtract one from the other. If you prefer paper, rule a page into the same three columns. Either way, keep it somewhere you will see it every week.

If a line is running high, decide now how to bring it back: spend less in that line next week or move money from a want.

Moving money from one line to another is allowed; that is what a living budget does. The two rules are: never move money out of savings for a non-emergency, and always write the change down so the plan stays honest.

If one line is over plan every single month, the plan is wrong, not you. Increase that line in next month's budget and reduce another line to keep the total balanced. After two or three months, your budget will reflect how your household really lives.
When someone asks for money

Requests from relatives, friends and neighbours are part of life. A clear **giving line** in your budget lets you respond calmly. When a request comes, check what is left in the giving line. If there is enough, give gladly. If not, you can offer a smaller amount, offer help in another form, or say kindly that you cannot this month. Taking from savings or rent money for non-emergencies is how many families fall behind.
Protect your digital money

Check your account balance before you spend, so you are never surprised. Turn on transaction alerts. Never share your PIN, password, OTP or BVN with anyone, including someone who says they are from your bank. Real banks do not ask for these by phone, SMS or WhatsApp.

Requests often come with urgency: "please, I need it today". Urgency is not the same as emergency. It is fine to say you will check your budget and reply in the evening. That short pause helps you decide calmly, and it protects you from scams that use urgent messages, sometimes from hacked accounts of friends, to rush people into sending money.

Celebrate small wins, such as a month where savings were fully protected.

No budget survives every month unchanged. Prices of food and fuel can rise quickly, a business can have a slow season, a spouse may lose work, or a family emergency may appear. A good budget is not rigid; it **bends without breaking**. This lesson shows you how to adjust calmly instead of abandoning the plan.

Decide now, while things are calm, what you will protect first if money becomes tight. A common order is shown below. Your family may differ, but writing it down in advance makes hard decisions faster.

When prices rise

When prices go up, your old food line will not buy the same basket. First, update the budget with real current prices from the market. Then look for substitutes and savings: buying staples in larger quantities with a neighbour, choosing local alternatives to costly items, cooking in larger batches to save gas, and comparing prices between markets. Then reduce wants to make room. Do not ignore the rise and hope; that is how overspending happens.
Worked example: a slow sales month
For example, Ngozi sells clothes in Onitsha. Her usual planning figure is about ₦150,000 a month, but sales are slow and she expects about ₦110,000 this month. That is a gap of about ₦40,000.
She cuts wants from ₦15,000 to ₦3,000, saving ₦12,000.
She reduces giving from ₦12,000 to ₦5,000, explaining to family that this is a tight month, saving ₦7,000.
She trims food from ₦55,000 to ₦49,000 by cooking in bulk and buying staples with a neighbour, saving ₦6,000.
She reduces her goal savings from ₦20,000 to ₦5,000, saving ₦15,000, but keeps paying rent savings in full.
The revised budget fits ₦110,000 without borrowing. When sales improve, she will restore her goal savings first.

Price rises also affect fixed lines over time. Rent may increase at renewal, school fees may rise at the start of a new session, and transport fares can change when fuel prices move. Ask early: talk to your landlord or the school bursar a few months before the due date, so you can raise your monthly saving in time rather than face a sudden shortfall.
Plan for heavy months you can predict

Some months are always expensive. January often follows festive spending and brings new school term costs. September has school resumption. December has festive costs and travel. Look at your calendar now and mark these months. Then add a small monthly saving line called "heavy months" so the money is ready. This turns a predictable crisis into a planned expense.

When an emergency hits mid-month

If an emergency happens in the middle of the month, follow three steps. First, use the emergency fund for the real cost, not a loan. Second, rewrite the remaining weeks of the budget with the lower amount of money left, cutting wants first. Third, add a rebuild line to next month's budget so the fund recovers. Writing the new plan down, even quickly, stops panic spending and keeps the family on track.
Pausing and restarting savings

In a true crisis, it can be reasonable to pause goal savings for a month or two to protect food and shelter. Try to keep at least a token amount going, even ₦500 a week, so the habit stays alive. Write down the date you will restart. When income recovers, restart savings before restoring wants.
Avoid the borrowing trap

When a month is tight, quick loans from apps or lenders can look like the answer. Borrowing for everyday food and bills, without a clear way to repay, usually makes the next month harder because of interest and fees. Use your emergency fund for real emergencies, adjust the budget, and see Module 4 for how to judge any loan carefully.

Most money problems are not caused by one big decision. They come from small habits repeated many times: a daily snack, a weekly bet, a monthly party outfit, lending without writing anything down. The good news is that habits can be changed, especially when you understand how they work.
How a habit works

Researchers who study behaviour often describe a habit as a loop with three parts. A **cue** is the trigger, such as payday, feeling stressed, seeing a WhatsApp status, or passing a particular shop. A **routine** is what you do, such as buying something. A **reward** is the good feeling you get afterwards. To change a habit, you keep the cue and the reward but swap the routine for a better one.

Lending to family and friends

Helping others is part of our culture, and it is good. But informal lending causes a lot of hidden money stress. Use these rules. Give, rather than lend, when you can afford it and do not expect it back. When you lend, lend only an amount you could survive losing. Write down the amount, date and agreed repayment date, and send a friendly WhatsApp message confirming it so there is a record. Do not lend from your emergency fund or rent savings.

If someone does not repay, decide calmly whether to remind them once, accept the loss, or agree a smaller repayment plan. Do not lend again to someone who has not repaid. Protecting your relationship and your household budget at the same time is easier when the rules are clear from the start.

Work out the true cost

Before borrowing, ask for three numbers in writing: **how much you receive**, **how much you must pay back in total**, and **by when**. The difference between what you receive and what you repay is the real cost. Some lenders deduct fees upfront, so you receive less than the loan amount but repay the full amount plus interest.
Worked example: comparing two loans
For example, Ruth needs about ₦50,000 to buy stock for her provisions shop. These offers are illustrative.
Loan A, a digital lender: she receives ₦50,000 and must repay ₦62,500 in 30 days. Cost: ₦12,500, which is 25 percent for just one month.
Loan B, her registered cooperative: she receives ₦50,000 and repays ₦5,500 a month for 10 months, a total of ₦55,000. Cost: ₦5,000 over 10 months.
She expects the stock to give her about ₦10,000 profit over the month.
With Loan A, the ₦12,500 cost is larger than her ₦10,000 profit, so she loses money.
With Loan B, she pays ₦5,500 a month from profits and still gains.
Ruth chooses Loan B. Comparing the total amount repaid, not just the monthly payment or the speed of approval, showed the real difference.
Digital loan apps: check before you borrow

Loan apps are fast, but some charge very high fees and some have abused borrowers' data. In Nigeria, digital lenders are regulated by the **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)**, which publishes a list of approved lenders on its website. Before borrowing, check that the app is on that list. Read which permissions the app requests. An app that wants access to all your contacts and photos is a warning sign. Shaming borrowers by messaging their contacts is not allowed, and you can report it to the FCCPC.
A person facing a warning sign
Pause at every warning sign: a genuine lender never needs your PIN or an upfront fee to a personal account.
Loan scams

**Advance fee scams:** someone promises a loan or grant but asks you to pay a "processing", "insurance" or "registration" fee first. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay to receive a loan into a personal account.
**Fake bank staff:** callers claim to be from your bank and ask for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP to "approve" a loan or "unblock" your account. Banks never ask for these.
**Fake government grants:** messages on WhatsApp or Facebook promising free government money if you pay a fee or share your details.
Ponzi schemes

A **ponzi scheme** pays earlier members using money from newer members, not from real business profits. It promises high, quick, often guaranteed returns, and it grows by recruitment. It always collapses when new money slows down, and most people, especially those who joined later, lose their money. In Nigeria, MMM Nigeria drew in large numbers of people before it froze members' accounts in December 2016, and many lost their savings.
Ponzi and scam warning signs

Guaranteed high returns. Pressure to act fast. Rewards for recruiting other people. Payment into a personal account. No registration with SEC Nigeria. One of these signs is enough reason to stop and check; several together almost always mean fraud.

Ponzi schemes often look convincing at first. Early members really are paid, and they share screenshots of their profits on WhatsApp and Facebook, which persuades friends and relatives to join. Some schemes use words like "crypto", "forex", "agriculture investment" or "mutual aid" to sound modern or kind. The label does not matter. Ask one question: where does the profit really come from? If nobody can show you a real, checkable business earning that money, keep your savings away.
Protect yourself

Check investment platforms with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria, lenders with the FCCPC, and banks with the CBN. Never share your PIN, password, OTP or full card details. If you have sent money to a fraudster, contact your bank immediately through its official channels and report to the police.

You have now learned to track, save, budget and borrow wisely. Goals bring these skills together and give them direction. A clear goal answers the question: what am I doing all this for? Without goals, saving feels like sacrifice. With goals, every naira saved is a step towards something you truly want.
Write SMART goals
A useful way to write goals is the **SMART** method. Each goal should be:
**Specific**: exactly what you want. "Buy a grinding machine for my pepper business", not "grow my business".
**Measurable**: an amount in naira, so you know when you have reached it.
**Achievable**: possible with your current income and budget, even if it takes time.
**Relevant**: important to you and your family, not to impress others.
**Time-bound**: a target date.

Long-term goals and investing

Some long-term goals, such as retirement, may later involve pensions or investments. Those carry their own risks and rules. Why this matters
Five money decisions
Earn: how money comes in
Spend: what you pay for
Save: what you keep for later
Borrow: using someone else's money
Protect: keeping safe from shocks and fraud
Financial literacy simply means understanding money well enough to make good choices with it. A market woman who knows what each bag of rice cost her is practising it every day.
Almost every money choice falls into one of five decisions. Earn is how money comes in.
Spend is what you pay for, and whether it is worth it.
Save is what you keep for later.
Borrow is when you use someone else's money, and at what cost.
And protect is keeping your money and family safe from shocks and fraud, like never sharing your BVN or OTP.
What happens if I do not buy it today?
Is there a cheaper version?
Can it wait 30 days?
Pay for needs first, save next, then enjoy wants.
A need keeps you safe, healthy and earning. A want makes life nicer but can wait.
Question one. What happens if I do not buy this today? If my family goes hungry, falls sick, loses shelter or I cannot work, it is a need.
Question two. Is there a cheaper version that meets the same need? Food is a need, but eating out every day is partly a want. The basic version is the need. The extra cost is the want.
Question three. Can it wait 30 days? Then write it on a wants list instead of buying it now. Many items drop off the list on their own.
Wants are not bad. A small planned treat is better than a big unplanned one that leaves you short for rent.

Include every channel: cash, transfers, POS, airtime and data, and money given to others.
Each week, group the spending into categories like food, transport and children. At month end, add each category and compare it with what you expected. The point is information, not guilt.

Why this matters
Give your savings a job
Protect the family from shocks
Reach goals bigger than one month's income
Seize good opportunities
Saving means keeping part of today's money for tomorrow. The secret is to give your savings a clear job. Money with a job is much easier to protect.
The first job is to protect the family from shocks, like illness or a broken shop freezer.
The second is to reach goals that cost more than one month's income, like rent or a sewing machine.
The third is to seize opportunities, like buying stock in bulk at a good price, without borrowing.
Work backwards from a goal

About 30,000 naira a month
About 7,000 naira a week

Save first, the moment money comes in. Spend after.
A real goal has an amount, a purpose and a date. For example, Kemi sells provisions in Abeokuta and wants a deep freezer costing about 300,000 naira. She sets a date 10 months away.
300,000 divided by 10 months is about 30,000 naira a month.
That is about 7,000 naira a week.
She already saves 3,000 a week, so she needs about 4,000 more.
From her tracking she cuts daily take-away lunch and buys shop stock in larger, cheaper quantities.
Most people save what is left at month end, and usually nothing is left. So pay yourself first. Move your savings out the moment money arrives, ideally by automatic transfer.
Where to save
Choose where to save by the job of the money. Safety first, access second, returns third.
Before you save anywhere, check these five things. If any answer is no or unclear, do not put your savings there. Money in an unlicensed scheme has no NDIC protection.
And keep savings in a separate account from your spending, with no debit card attached.

Saving with others: the real risks
Usually no insurance, and recovering the money is difficult.
A member stops paying after collecting, so later members receive less or nothing.
Disputes about who paid what. Keep a signed record book at every meeting.

Women have saved together for generations, in ajo, esusu, adashe and isusu. For example, ten market women in Ibadan each pay about 20,000 naira a month for ten months. Each month one woman collects about 200,000 naira.
But there are real risks. The collector can disappear with members' money.
A member can stop paying after collecting. Bisi drew number 2 and collected in month 2, but she must keep paying until month 10.
And poor records lead to disputes. Write the rules down, sign the record book at every meeting, and where possible keep group money in an account that needs two signatories.

Join only groups of people you know well and can find. In a real ajo, every member pays in and receives the same amount, with written rules and records.
Be very careful with anyone promising high guaranteed returns, or paying you to bring in new members.
Or asking you to pay into a personal account, or pressuring you to act fast. That is a ponzi scheme, not ajo.
And licensed banks never ask for your PIN, password or OTP.

An emergency fund is money kept only for real, unexpected problems, like sudden illness or losing your main customer. Rent and school fees are not emergencies. They get their own pots.

Why this matters
Tell your money what to do
A budget is a plan made before you spend
Tracking looks back; a budget looks forward
Decide calmly, not under pressure
A budget is a plan for your money, made before you spend it. This much is coming in, and this is exactly where it will go.
Tracking looks back at what happened. A budget looks forward. Together they form a loop: plan, spend, track, compare, improve.
A budget is not a punishment or a sign that you are poor. It means you decide in advance, calmly, instead of at the market or when a relative calls.

A popular guideline is 50 percent for needs, 30 percent for wants, and 20 percent for savings.
For example, Zainab, a nurse in Abuja, takes home about 250,000 naira a month. The classic split gives needs 125,000, wants 75,000 and savings 50,000.
But her real needs, including her mother's medicine, are about 175,000. That is 70 percent, and that is not failure.
So she cuts wants to 25,000 and keeps savings at 50,000. She protects her savings by trimming wants, not by pretending her needs are smaller.
Line by line
Fill your budget in this order
Income at the top
Savings first: pay yourself
Fixed needs: rent savings, fees
Variable needs: food, transport, gas
Giving, wants and a small buffer
Add up and balance
Never balance a budget by borrowing for everyday needs.
Write your expected income at the top. Use take-home pay, or your safe figure if income is irregular. Then write savings first.
Then fixed needs. Turn yearly costs like rent into a monthly line, so the money is waiting when the rent date comes.
Then variable needs, using your tracking as a guide.
Then a realistic giving line for church or mosque, family and events. Wants should be modest but not zero. And add a buffer of about 5 percent for things you forgot.
If the total is more than income, cut wants first, then trim variable needs. If it still does not balance, income may need to rise.
Do not borrow for everyday needs. That only moves the problem to next month, with interest added.

Why this matters
Small habits, repeated many times
Cue: the trigger
Routine: what you do
Reward: the good feeling
Swap the routine, keep the reward
Most money problems come from small habits repeated many times: a daily snack, a weekly bet, lending without writing anything down.
A habit is a loop. The cue is the trigger, like payday or a WhatsApp status.
The routine is what you do, such as buying something.
The reward is the good feeling afterwards.
To change a habit, keep the cue and the reward, but swap the routine for a better one.

Before borrowing, ask for three numbers in writing: how much you receive, how much you repay in total, and by when.

For example, Ruth needs about 50,000 naira for stock. A digital lender wants 62,500 back in 30 days. That costs 12,500, which is 25 percent for one month. The stock will earn her only about 10,000, so she would lose money.
Her registered cooperative wants 5,500 a month for 10 months, 55,000 in total. The cost is 5,000 naira, and she still gains. Ruth chooses Loan B.
Compare the total amount repaid, not just the monthly payment or the speed of approval.
Three scams to know
A loan or grant that needs a processing fee first. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay to receive a loan.
Callers asking for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP. Banks never ask for these.
Old members paid with new members' money. It always collapses, and most people lose.
Know these three scams. First, someone promises a loan or grant but asks for a processing, insurance or registration fee first. Do not pay.
Second, callers claim to be from your bank and ask for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP. Banks never ask for these.
Third, ponzi schemes. They pay earlier members with money from newer members, not real profits. MMM Nigeria froze members' accounts in December 2016, and many lost their savings.
Warning signs are guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, rewards for recruiting, payment into a personal account, and no registration with SEC Nigeria.

If you have sent money to a fraudster, contact your bank immediately through its official channels and report to the police. And if betting is taking over in your home, delete the apps, tell a trusted person, and seek support.
